newsitem.title: UK: Brent Spar legacy - small firms buy old oilfields.
newsitem.headline: Brent Spar legacy - small firms buy old oilfields.

text.p: Small oil exploration companies without retail operations in Britain are buying up ageing U.K. oilfields in the wake of last year's Brent Spar controversy, a leading North Sea consultancy said on Friday.
Oil companies operating in British waters face an 8.7 billion stg pre-tax bill stretched out over the next 35 years to decommission ageing oilfields, said Edinburgh-based Wood Mackenzie in a report.
Royal Dutch/Shell, still seeking a solution for its controversial Brent Spar platform, faces the largest bill -- 1.2 billion stg at today's prices, excluding tax relief.

Shell is examining a number of options for the Spar after being forced last year to rethink its plans to ditch the storage and loading buoy in the Atlantic by an environmental campaign led by Greenpeace.
Abandonment costs for British Petroleum and Exxon Corp are likely to hit 1.1 billion stg apiece and for British Gas 585 million stg.
But mature North Sea fields are being sold by the oil majors to smaller companies keen to squeeze more out of assets the bigger companies no longer thought worthwhile, Woodmac said.
And without retail operations, the exploration-only operators would not face the same public relations pressures as Shell in the Brent Spar case.

"Companies which do not have a retailing presence will not be so susceptible and exposed to public pressure and consumer boycott as those companies that do," Woodmac said. "The issues of disposal have less potential impact on a company's balance sheet and reputation."
Some smaller companies had made a strategic decision to focus on short-term production from mature fields, reducing corporate debt while increasing exposure to abandonment costs, the report said.
Canadian Talisman Energy Inc in August agreed to buy three British Petroleum North Sea fields. As a result the company's exposure to abandonment costs has risen from 55 million stg to 149 million.
United States Oryx Energy Co acquired its first U.K. oil operatorship in 1994 and over the last two years has increased its liability to abandonment by 33 percent to 254 million stg.
U.S. Conoco and Chevron reduced abandonment costs by 15 percent to 217 million stg and 28 percent to 97 million respectively.

"As the oil majors look to maintain and increase value from their U.K. operations by bringing new fields onstream combined with moving out to frontier regins opportunities will continue for "second tier' companies to acquire mature assets," the report said.
Technological advances in production, seismic surveys and drilling techniques and cost reduction efforts have increased oilfield longevity and raised reservoir estimates.
Woodmac said tax relief was likely to save oil companies a sizeable chunk of total decommissioning costs.

"The final abandonment liability for each company will be significantly less as provisions for the clawback of tax from the U.K. tax payer occurs," Woodmac said. For 71 companies holding oil or gas assets in British waters the average total abandonment provision now stands at 123 million stg.
Expenditure on the abandonment of some 223 facilities was likely to peak between 2007 and 2018, Woodmac said.

Twenty structures have already been decommissioned to date and a further 14 fields were expected to abandon before the turn of the century, the consultancy said. --Richard Mably, London newsroom +44 171 542 8060
